extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Restoration drama; playwrights and scholars of 17th-century English theatre
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical observations for producing and evaluating English Restoration plays (stage success, audience taste, prologues, originality, patronage, and performance). Useful for playwrights, critics, and students of 17th-century drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality (mode over subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: "originality consists in the mode of treating a subject, more than in the subject itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation of subjects or sources is not necessarily plagiarism; what matters is the poet's manner of treatment. Langbaine's attacks that focus on identical subject-matter miss this point. Examples on the page: alleged imitations from Scarron and other novels do not prove lack of originality if the handling differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance success factors
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whether the fault was in the play itself, or in the lameness of the action, or in the number of its enemies, who came resolved to damn it for the title..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play's public failure can stem from the text, its staging (a 'lameness of the action'), or pre-existing hostility among critics/audience. Evaluation of a play should consider these separate contributors rather than assume the text alone is to blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedications and patronage (use with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The design of dedicating plays is as common and unjust, as that of desiring seconds in a duel. It is engaging our friends... in a senseless quarrel where they have much to venture..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dedications are a social strategy to gain favour/reputation, but they risk involving patrons in quarrels or obliging them to defend the work. Authors should be modest in demanding time or defence from patrons; dedications are a practical, not purely literary, tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect classical predecessors and demonstrate learning
rubrics_metrics.description: "no man can pretend to be a poet" without learning; Dryden stresses praising and understanding predecessors: "I know I honour Ben Jonson... because, without vanity I may own, I understand him better."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A competent poet/playwright should show knowledge of earlier masters and be able to criticise with informed taste. Openly attacking predecessors risks being misunderstood; acknowledging and understanding sources strengthens credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate tasteful conviviality (eruditam voluptatem)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poets of the ancients "pursued an innocent and inoffensive pleasure... genial nights, where our discourse is neither too serious nor too light, but always pleasant, and, for the most part, instructive".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary life and presentation should aim for balanced, cultured entertainment — witty and instructive without being scandalously censorious. This informs tone and social positioning of both author and work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blasphemy and atheism as cheap provocation
rubrics_metrics.description: "For blasphemy and atheism, if they were neither sin nor ill manners, are subjects so very common, and worn so threadbare, that people, who have sense, avoid them, for fear of being suspected to have none."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on blasphemy or ostentatious irreligion is an exhausted tactic that reflects poorly on the author's judgment. Such material is an anti-pattern in seeking serious literary respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prologue's role: frame, defend, and preempt audience/censor
rubrics_metrics.description: "Prologues, like bells to churches, toll you in... You damned the poet, but the priest damns you... Pardon our poet, if he speaks his mind; You come to plays with your own follies lined."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prologue should prepare the audience, acknowledge and deflect likely criticisms, and employ wit to preempt hostile readings. It can call out audience follies, defend the poet's intentions, and set expectations for the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirror audience follies to secure engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: "You must have Mamamouchi... Where, rain'd in crowds, you see yourselves in him."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plays that present recognizable follies or fashionable figures (so audiences see themselves in the character) attract and satisfy crowds. However, there is risk in showing too close a likeness to real persons; use recognition strategically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and write to contemporary fashions (fops and buffoonery)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Th' unnatural strained buffoon is only taking; No fop can please you now of God's own making."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience appetite for particular comic types (exaggerated fops, strained buffoonery) determines popularity. Playwrights should be aware of current fashions and craft characters that meet those expectations when desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spectacle and noisy show to draw and sustain crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: "plays of rhyme and noise, with wondrous show:-- Then shall the house... Be for at least six months full every day."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extravagant stage effects, pageantry, and noisy spectacle can keep a play popular for an extended run. This is a practical production consideration: spectacle may compensate for other weaknesses in attracting audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical interludes, jargon, and nonsense may please
rubrics_metrics.description: Ravenscroft's pieces featured "the jargon of the songs... like similar nonsense of our own day, seems to have been well received on the stage."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonsense refrains, foreign-sounding jargon, and dance-songs inserted into plays can delight audiences and become popular elements even if they are unsubstantial literarily; consider their strategic use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and account for critics' biases (pedants and malice)
rubrics_metrics.description: "they paint lewdness, atheism, folly, ill-reasoning, and all manner of extravagancies amongst us, for want of understanding what we are... Oftentimes it so falls out, that they have a particular pique to some one amongst us, and then they immediately interest heaven in their quarrel."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism often comes from misunderstanding, envy, or institutional bias. Writers should recognise these motives, avoid taking every attack as purely literary, and address misreadings where useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors' readiness and style affect audience reception
rubrics_metrics.description: "To act their parts, the players were ashamed..." and earlier: actors might be 'ashamed' to act certain parts, affecting reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting, actors' willingness to embody roles, and the perceived quality of acting are decisive to stage success. Textual quality is inseparable from its enactment; poor acting or reluctance can ruin otherwise good material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance wit with moderation and avoid excessive censoriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: "the raillery, neither too sharp upon the present, nor too censorious on the absent; and the cups only such as will raise the conversation of the night, without disturbing the business of the morrow."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit should be pointed but measured: too sharp satire or overly censorious tone alienates audiences or invites moral censure. Social and rhetorical moderation preserves reputation and collegiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include fools/comic figures but avoid making them unrelatable
rubrics_metrics.description: "You must have fools, yet none will have himself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic figures are essential to comedy, but playwrights must craft them so audiences enjoy the folly without feeling personally attacked. The paradox: audiences want fools on stage but resist seeing themselves exposed as such.
